newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin to plead for time in policy speech.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin to plead for time in policy speech.

text.p: New French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin was expected to plead for time in his keynote policy statement on Thursday, saying his left-wing government needs to know the true state of public finances from an independent audit before it can implement most of its election promises.

Government sources said Jospin would announce to parliament a timetable for meeting some key pledges but defer most until after auditors report in mid-July on how far France's deficit has strayed from the target of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) to qualify for a single European currency.

Trade unions are looking to the Socialist leader to announce a significant increase in the 6,400-francs-a-month ($1,095) national minimum wage and a cut in Value Added Tax on basic goods such as bread.
He is also expected to pledge to free France's tarnished justice system from government meddling and scrap or modify several public works projects to meet environmental concerns.

But the government said on Wednesday that a mini-budget would be put off until September at the earliest, and a planned national conference to negotiate trade-offs between wages, jobs and working hours is also likely to wait until the autumn.

After tough negotiations at a European Union summit in Amsterdam on his demands for a shift in focus of EU policy from strict monetarism to boosting jobs and growth, Jospin is expected to reaffirm his commitment to launching the euro on time in 1999.

But newspapers said on Thursday the incoming goverment faced a far bigger public deficit than its centre-right predecessors had admitted, making it harder for Jospin to keep campaign pledges without pushing France off course for monetary union.

The daily Liberation said the social security deficit, a key component of France's total public deficit, could hit 42 to 45 billion francs this year and Le Monde said it could be in a range from 40 to 50 billion francs.
Those figures, not confirmed officially, compared with the outgoing government's budget forecast of 30 billion francs and last estimate of 35 billion francs.
Liberation said weak revenue rather than overspending on health and welfare benefits explained the larger gap.
French financial markets were steady ahead of the speech, starting at 3 p.m. (1300 GMT).
Jospin has said he wants a flexible reading of the Maastricht treaty criteria for a single currency and pledged there would be no extra austerity measures to meet the target.
Government sources have confirmed the existence of a note by the finance ministry's budget division pointing to a risk of the total public deficit reaching 3.5 percent of GDP.
Le Monde said in April the note also contained a "worst case scenario" where the total public deficit could hit 3.8 percent of GDP, with a social security deficit of 47 billion in 1997.
Pending the audit, Jospin was expected to give only limited insight into economic figures in his keynote speech.

Trade unions and financial markets will be watching how he sets about fulfilling an election promise to create 700,000 new jobs for young people, half of them in the public sector. He also aims to cut the working week from 39 hours to 35 over five years with no loss of pay.
After his address, Jospin will ask the National Assembly for a vote of confidence in his pink-red-green government, which took office after an upset victory in the June 1 election.
Routine approval is assured since the Socialists, Communists and Greens hold a comfortable majority.
